mainEntity.name: What is a switch statement in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A switch statement in Java is a multi-way branch control flow statement that evaluates an expression and executes the matching case block. It is an alternative to a long if-else-if chain when testing a single variable against multiple constant values. Syntax: switch (expression) { case value1: statements; break; case value2: statements; break; default: statements; }. The switch expression can be int, byte, short, char, String (Java 7+), or enum. Without break, execution falls through to the next case. The default case runs when no case matches.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between switch statement and switch expression in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Switch statement (classic): used for control flow — executes a block of statements. Does not produce a value. Requires break to prevent fall-through. Introduced in early Java. Switch expression (Java 14+): produces a value that can be assigned or returned. Uses arrow labels (case X ->) that prevent fall-through automatically. Or uses traditional colon labels with yield to return a value. Exhaustiveness is required for switch expressions — every possible value must be covered (with default or all enum values). Switch expressions are more concise, safer (no accidental fall-through), and expression-oriented.

mainEntity.name: What is fall-through in Java switch?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fall-through is the behaviour where execution continues from a matched case into the next case without stopping, because there is no break statement. Example: switch(x) { case 1: System.out.println('one'); case 2: System.out.println('two'); } — if x=1, both 'one' and 'two' are printed. Fall-through is usually unintentional and a bug. It can occasionally be used intentionally to share code between cases. Enhanced switch (Java 14+) arrow labels (case X ->) do not fall through — each arrow case is independent. Always use break in classic switch cases to prevent accidental fall-through.

mainEntity.name: Can we use String in switch in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — String is supported in switch from Java 7 onwards. Example: switch (day) { case 'Monday': ...; break; case 'Tuesday': ...; break; default: ...; }. The comparison uses .equals() internally — it is case-sensitive ('Monday' and 'monday' are different cases). Null safety: passing null to a switch expression throws NullPointerException — always null-check before switching on a String. Switch can also use: byte, short, int, char, their wrapper classes (Byte, Short, Integer, Character), String (Java 7+), enum, and patterns (Java 21+). long, float, double, and boolean are NOT supported as switch selectors.

mainEntity.name: What is the yield keyword in Java switch?

acceptedAnswer.text: yield (Java 14+) is used inside a switch expression with traditional colon-style case blocks to produce (return) a value from the switch expression. It is similar to return but only for switch expressions. Example: int result = switch (day) { case MONDAY -> 1; case TUESDAY: yield 2; default: yield 0; }; yield is required when a case in a switch expression uses a colon label and contains multiple statements. For arrow labels (->), yield is not needed — the expression after -> is the value. yield is not a keyword for regular switch statements — only switch expressions.

sections.title: What is a Switch Statement in Java?

blocks.text: A switch statement is a control flow construct that evaluates a single expression and branches execution to the matching case label. It is a cleaner alternative to a long if-else-if chain when you are comparing one variable against multiple constant values. Instead of writing condition after condition, switch lets you list each possible value as a distinct case and execute the corresponding block.

Java's switch has evolved significantly across versions: the classic switch statement (all Java versions) handles control flow with explicit break statements and optional fall-through. The enhanced switch expression (Java 14+) produces a value, uses concise arrow syntax, and eliminates fall-through by default. The pattern matching switch (Java 21) adds type patterns and guarded conditions, making switch a powerful tool for data-driven dispatch.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Switch at a Glance
blocks.text: Classic switch statement: uses case: (colon) labels. Requires break to stop fall-through. Does not produce a value. Works since Java 1. Enhanced switch expression: uses case -> (arrow) labels. No fall-through. Produces a value. Java 14+. yield keyword: returns a value from a multi-statement case block in a switch expression. Java 14+. Pattern matching switch: case with type patterns (case Dog d) and guards (when d.age() > 2). Java 21+. Supported selector types: byte, short, int, char, their wrappers, String (Java 7+), enum, and any reference type (Java 21+ patterns). NOT supported: long, float, double, boolean.

The classic switch statement has a straightforward structure: the keyword switch, followed by the selector expression in parentheses, followed by a block containing one or more case labels, an optional default label, and statements. Each case matches a constant value — not a range or condition — and execution jumps to the matching label.

blocks.label: SwitchSyntax.java
lines: //     default:         // Optional — runs if no case matches
// 1. case values must be compile-time constants (literals or final vars)
// 2. case values must be unique — no duplicate case labels
// 4. default can appear anywhere — not just at the end
// 5. Multiple statements allowed per case without braces
// 6. Empty case (no statements) falls through to the next case
case JAN:  // ✅ Allowed — JAN is a compile-time constant (final)

blocks.title: ⚠️ Case Values Must Be Compile-Time Constants
blocks.text: Every case label must be a compile-time constant — a literal value (1, 'A', "Monday"), an enum constant, or a final primitive variable initialized with a literal. A non-final variable is NOT allowed as a case value: int x = 5; case x: — compile error. A final variable IS allowed: final int X = 5; case X: — valid. Duplicate case values cause a compile error. This restriction exists because the JVM uses a lookup table (tableswitch / lookupswitch bytecode) for switch — all case values must be known at compile time for this optimization.

Understanding the execution flow of a switch is essential — especially the role of break and fall-through. When a switch is executed: (1) The selector expression is evaluated once. (2) Java compares the result against each case label from top to bottom. (3) When a match is found, execution jumps to that case and runs the statements. (4) Execution continues downward through subsequent cases until a break, return, or the end of the switch block is reached. (5) If no case matches, the default case runs (if present).

blocks.label: SwitchFlow.java
lines: // ── Normal flow: break stops execution at each case ───────────────
// ── No default, no match — switch does nothing ────────────────────
// ── default NOT at the end — still only runs if no case matches ────
// Output: Three  (case 3 matches — default skipped even though it's first)
// ── return inside switch — exits the method ───────────────────────
return "Weekday";   // return acts like break + exits method

blocks.text: The break statement is used inside a classic switch to exit the switch block after a case executes. Without break, execution falls through to the next case — regardless of whether it matches — and continues until a break, return, or the end of the switch block is reached. This fall-through behaviour is a notorious source of bugs. Every case in a classic switch should end with break (or return) unless fall-through is deliberately intended.

blocks.label: BreakInSwitch.java
lines: case 2: System.out.println("Two");   break;  // ← Exits after this
// ── break exits only the switch, not an outer loop ────────────────
break;  // Exits the switch, NOT the for loop
// ── return instead of break — exits the entire method ────────────
case 2: return "Two";   // return exits method — no fall-through

blocks.text: The default case is the switch equivalent of the else clause in an if-else chain. It executes when none of the case labels match the selector value. It is optional but strongly recommended — omitting it means unmatched values silently do nothing, which can hide bugs. The default case can appear anywhere in the switch block — not just at the end — but placing it last is the universally followed convention for readability. For switch expressions, default is usually required to ensure exhaustiveness.

blocks.label: DefaultCase.java
lines: // ── default at the end — conventional position ────────────────────
// ── default at the top — valid but unconventional ─────────────────
// Output: Default runs  (val=5 matches no case — default executes)
case 1:  System.out.println("One"); // No break — falls through
// Default also runs   (fall-through from case 1 into default)
// ── Switch expression — default required for exhaustiveness ─────────
default    -> "F";  // Required — int has infinite possible values

blocks.title: 💡 Always Include default
blocks.text: Always include a default case in every switch — even if you believe all possible values are covered. A switch without default silently does nothing for unmatched values — no error, no warning. This makes bugs hard to detect. In a switch expression, the compiler enforces exhaustiveness: if you do not cover all possible values, it is a compile error. For switch statements, it is the programmer's responsibility to add default. Convention: place default last. If you intentionally want to do nothing for unmatched values, add an explicit comment: default: // intentionally empty.

Fall-through is the behaviour where, after a matched case executes, control continues into the next case without stopping — because there is no break. It is one of the most notorious Java pitfalls for beginners and experienced developers alike. However, fall-through is occasionally used intentionally to share code between consecutive cases — for example, grouping multiple values that produce the same result.

blocks.label: FallThrough.java
lines: // This is a BUG — programmer forgot break statements

blocks.title: ⚠️ Fall-Through Is Usually a Bug
blocks.text: Most real-world fall-through occurrences are bugs — a forgotten break. The enhanced switch expression (Java 14+) with arrow labels eliminates fall-through entirely — each arrow case is independent. When using classic switch, always end every case with break, return, throw, or continue (if inside a loop). If fall-through is genuinely intentional, add a comment: // fall through intentional and consider the @SuppressWarnings('fallthrough') annotation. Code reviewers will ask about any case without break — be prepared to justify it.

When multiple values should produce the same result, Java allows grouping case labels so they share a single block of code. In classic switch, this is done by stacking empty cases on top of each other (intentional fall-through). In enhanced switch (Java 14+), the cleaner approach is using comma-separated case labels: case 1, 2, 3 ->. The comma syntax is only available in enhanced switch (Java 14+) — it is not valid in classic switch colon-style cases.

blocks.label: MultipleCaseLabels.java
lines: default        -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid month: " + month);

blocks.text: Since Java 7, String is a valid selector type in switch. Before Java 7, only integral types and enum were allowed. String switch uses .equals() internally for comparison — it is case-sensitive ("Monday" and "monday" are different cases). A critical safety rule: always null-check before switching on a String — if the String is null, the switch throws a NullPointerException.

blocks.label: StringInSwitch.java
lines: // ✅ Always null-check before switching on String

blocks.title: 📌 How String Switch Works Internally
blocks.text: The compiler translates String switch into two-stage logic: first, it calls hashCode() on the selector String to find the right bucket (fast O(1) lookup), then calls equals() to verify the match (handles hash collisions). This means String switch is efficient even with many cases. But it also explains why it is case-sensitive — equals() on String is case-sensitive. To make String switch case-insensitive, always normalize the selector before switching: switch (input.trim().toUpperCase()) { case 'START': ... }. Java 21 pattern matching switch also handles null directly — see the null in switch section.

sections.title: Enum in Switch — The Cleanest Switch Pattern

blocks.text: Using an enum as the switch selector is one of the most powerful and clean patterns in Java. Enums provide a closed, compile-time-known set of values — the compiler can verify exhaustiveness and warn if new enum constants are not handled. When all enum constants are covered in cases, default is not needed (though still recommended for future-proofing). Enum in switch is the preferred approach when a variable can take one of a fixed set of named states.

blocks.label: EnumInSwitch.java
lines: enum Day { MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, FRIDAY, SATURDAY, SUNDAY }
enum OrderStatus { PENDING, CONFIRMED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }
// Note: no 'default' needed — all enum values covered
case MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, FRIDAY -> "9 AM - 5 PM";
// No default needed — all enum constants covered (exhaustive)
case PENDING   -> "Your order is awaiting confirmation.";
case CONFIRMED -> "Your order has been confirmed!";
case SHIPPED   -> "Your order is on the way!";
case DELIVERED -> "Your order has been delivered. Enjoy!";
case CANCELLED -> "Your order has been cancelled.";
// Output: Your order is on the way!
// ── Enum switch with method body — multi-statement ────────────────

blocks.title: 💡 Enum + Switch Expression = Best Combination
blocks.text: Enum with enhanced switch expression is the gold standard for state/status-based branching in Java. The compiler guarantees exhaustiveness — if you add a new enum constant later and forget to handle it in the switch expression, it becomes a compile error immediately. This is far safer than if-else chains or String switches which silently fall to default when new values are added. In switch expression covering all enum constants, you can omit default — but many teams keep it for defensive programming and to handle future constants gracefully.

Java 14 introduced the switch expression as a standard feature (JEP 361). Unlike the classic switch statement (which executes code), a switch expression produces a value that can be assigned, returned, or used in another expression. Switch expressions use arrow labels (case X ->) that eliminate fall-through by default, require exhaustiveness (covering all possible values), and are significantly more concise than the classic form.

blocks.label: EnhancedSwitchExpression.java
lines: // ── Basic switch expression — produces a value ────────────────────
default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown month: " + month);
// ── Switch expression: no fall-through — each arrow case independent
case 2 -> "Two";    // Only this executes — no fall-through
return switch (day) {          // switch expression returned directly

blocks.title: 📌 Switch Expression Rules
blocks.text: Must be exhaustive — every possible value must be covered (use default for non-enum types). Produces a value — can be used in assignments, returns, method arguments. No fall-through with arrow labels — each case -> is independent. Semicolon after closing brace when assigned: String s = switch(...) { ... };. Can throw exceptions in cases: default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException('...'). Can use yield in colon-style cases to produce a value from a multi-statement block. All case arms must produce the same type (or compatible types).

Arrow labels (case X ->) are the new concise syntax introduced in Java 14. They replace the traditional case X: colon syntax with three key improvements: no fall-through (each arrow case is self-contained), concise single-line expressions (no need for break), and block support for multi-statement cases using yield. Arrow labels can be used in both switch expressions and switch statements.

blocks.label: ArrowLabels.java
lines: case 1 -> "One";    // Expression after -> is the value
// ── Arrow label: block body with yield ────────────────────────────
// Multi-statement block — use yield to produce value
yield base;  // yield returns the value from this block
// ── Arrow label in switch STATEMENT (not expression) ──────────────
// Arrow labels can also be used without assigning a value
// ── Comparison: old style vs arrow style ─────────────────────────
// NEW (arrow switch expression) — same result, more concise:

blocks.text: The yield keyword (Java 14+) is used inside a switch expression to produce (return) a value from a multi-statement case block. It is analogous to return but scoped to the switch expression — it does not exit the enclosing method. yield is only valid in switch expressions, not in switch statements. When using arrow labels (->) with a single expression, yield is implicit and not needed. yield is only required when a case uses a {} block body with multiple statements.

blocks.label: YieldKeyword.java
lines: yield "B";  // yield provides the value for this case block
// ── yield in colon-style case (traditional labels in switch expression)
yield base + bonus;   // yield — provides value to switch expression
// return base + bonus; // ❌ Would exit the method, not just switch
return baseDiscount;  // return exits the method

blocks.title: 📌 yield — Key Rules
blocks.text: yield is only valid inside a switch expression — not in a switch statement. yield produces the value of the switch expression for that case — it does not exit the method. In an arrow case (case X -> value), yield is implicit — you do not need to write yield. In a block arrow case (case X -> { ... }) or colon-style case, yield is required to supply the value. You cannot use break in a switch expression the way you would in a statement — use yield instead. yield is not a keyword in switch statements — it causes a compile error if used there. yield is a context-sensitive keyword — it can still be used as a variable or method name outside switch expressions (not recommended).

sections.title: switch vs if-else — When to Use Which

blocks.text: Both switch and if-else handle multi-way branching, but each has strengths and appropriate use cases. The key difference: switch tests a single expression against constant values, while if-else can test arbitrary conditions including ranges, compound conditions, and non-constant comparisons.

blocks.label: SwitchVsIfElse.java
lines: // ── USE switch: many values of a single variable ──────────────────
// ── USE if-else: ranges and compound conditions ───────────────────
// switch CANNOT do this — no range support:
// if-else is the correct choice for ranges:
// ── USE switch expression to assign result ────────────────────────
// if-else equivalent is more verbose for assignment:

blocks.text: Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441, standard in Java 21) extends switch to work with type patterns — the same patterns used in instanceof. This allows you to test what type an object is AND bind it to a typed variable in one step, inside a switch. It is the modern, exhaustive, and null-safe alternative to long chains of if (x instanceof TypeA a) ... else if (x instanceof TypeB b). Combined with guarded patterns (when clauses) and sealed class hierarchies, pattern matching switch is extremely powerful.

blocks.label: PatternMatchingSwitch.java
lines: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height)   implements Shape {}
case String  s  -> "String of length " + s.length();
case Circle    c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
// No default needed — sealed hierarchy is exhaustive
// ── Pattern matching: replaces long instanceof chain ───────────────
// else if (data instanceof Double d) { System.out.println(d * 2); }
// else if (data instanceof String s) { System.out.println(s.toUpperCase()); }
// ── Payment type dispatch with pattern matching ───────────────────
sealed interface Payment permits CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment {}
record CreditCardPayment(double amount, String last4) implements Payment {}
record UPIPayment(double amount, String upiId)        implements Payment {}

blocks.text: A guarded pattern adds an extra boolean condition to a type pattern using the when keyword. The case only matches if the type check AND the boolean condition both pass. This eliminates the need for nested if statements inside pattern match cases, making complex type-and-condition dispatch extremely concise. The when clause has access to the bound variable from the pattern.

blocks.label: GuardedPatterns.java
lines: case Integer i when i < 0     -> "Negative integer: " + i;
case String  s when s.isEmpty() -> "Empty string";
record Product(String name, double price, int stock) {}
case Product p when p.stock() == 0  -> p.name() + " is OUT OF STOCK";
case Product p when p.stock() < 5   -> p.name() + " is LOW STOCK ("+p.stock()+" left)";
case Product p when p.price() > 50000 -> p.name() + " is PREMIUM (₹"+p.price()+")";
// Output: Laptop is OUT OF STOCK
// ── Guarded patterns eliminate nested if inside case ──────────────
record User(String name, String role, boolean isActive) {}
case User u when u.role().equals("ADMIN") -> u.name() + " — Full Access";
case User u when u.role().equals("EDITOR") -> u.name() + " — Edit Access";
case User u                             -> u.name() + " — Read Only";

blocks.title: 💡 Guarded Pattern Ordering — More Specific First
blocks.text: When using guarded patterns, order your cases from most specific to least specific. The switch checks cases top-to-bottom and the first match wins. If a less specific case appears before a more specific one, the more specific case becomes unreachable and the compiler will warn you. Example: case Integer i -> 'any int' before case Integer i when i > 0 -> 'positive' — the second case is dead code. Always put guarded patterns (with when) before unguarded patterns of the same type: case Integer i when i < 0 (specific) before case Integer i (general catch-all).

In classic switch (all versions) and enhanced switch without pattern matching, passing null as the selector throws a NullPointerException. Java 21 pattern matching switch adds explicit case null support — you can handle the null case directly inside the switch instead of wrapping the switch in a null check. This makes pattern matching switch the first switch form that is fully null-safe when case null is included.

blocks.label: SwitchWithNull.java
lines: // ── Java 21: case null inside pattern matching switch ─────────────
case null, default -> System.out.println("Null or unmatched");
// ── Practical: API response handling with null ────────────────────

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Switch Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These are the most frequent switch-related mistakes in Java — from forgotten breaks to type confusion and null traps.

blocks.label: SwitchMistakes.java
lines: // ✅ Fix: add break after every case, or use enhanced switch
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Using non-constant in case label
// switch (x) { case limit: ... }  // ❌ Compile error — limit is not final
// ✅ Fix: make it final: final int LIMIT = 10;
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Switching on null String — NullPointerException
// ✅ Fix: null-check first, or use Java 21 case null
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Using long, float, double, boolean as switch selector
// switch (l) { ... }    // ❌ Compile error — long not supported
// switch (f) { ... }    // ❌ Compile error — float not supported
// ✅ Supported: byte, short, int, char, String, enum, and patterns (Java 21)
//     case 5: ...;  // ❌ Compile error: duplicate case label
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Missing default in switch expression — compile error
//     // ❌ Compile error: switch expression does not cover all possible input values
// ✅ Fix: normalize before switch: switch (day.substring(0,1).toUpperCase() + day.substring(1).toLowerCase())
// ❌ MISTAKE 8: Using return in switch statement thinking it exits switch
// return inside a switch in a void method is a compile error.
// return exits the METHOD, not just the switch.
// In non-void methods it is valid — and acts like break + exits the method.
// ❌ MISTAKE 9: yield used in switch statement (not expression)
//     case 1: yield "One"; // ❌ Compile error — yield only in switch expression
// ❌ MISTAKE 10: Ordering pattern cases — less specific before more specific
//     case Integer i  -> ...;           // Catches ALL integers
//     case Integer i when i > 0 -> ...; // ❌ Unreachable — compiler warning

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns around switch usage indicate poor design decisions that make code harder to read, maintain, and extend.

items.title: Using switch for Range Conditions
items.text: Writing switch (score / 10) { case 10: ... case 9: ... } is a workaround to simulate range testing in switch. While it works for simple cases, it is fragile — what if score is negative? What if the range changes? If the condition is inherently a range (score >= 90), use if-else which expresses intent directly. Reserve switch for matching against specific discrete values, not ranges coerced into discrete form.

items.title: Classic Switch Without default
items.text: Omitting default from a classic switch statement means unmatched values silently do nothing — no error, no log, nothing. This makes runtime bugs invisible. Every classic switch should have a default case, even if it just logs an unexpected value or throws an exception. In switch expressions, the compiler enforces exhaustiveness — missing cases cause compile errors. Apply the same discipline to switch statements manually.

items.title: Intentional Fall-Through Without Comment
items.text: Writing consecutive cases without break and without a comment explaining the intention. Any reader (including future-you) will assume it is a bug and add a break, breaking your logic. If fall-through is genuinely intentional, always add: // fall through — intentional. Consider also using the @SuppressWarnings('fallthrough') annotation and a descriptive comment. Better yet, use enhanced switch comma-separated labels (case 1, 2, 3 ->) which express grouping without any fall-through risk.

items.title: String Switch Without Null Check
items.text: Switching on a String variable that could be null without a prior null check is a latent NullPointerException. In classic and Java 14 enhanced switch, null always causes NPE. Never switch on an externally-supplied String (from user input, API responses, databases) without null handling: if (s == null) { ... } before the switch, or use Java 21 case null in a pattern matching switch.

items.title: Massive Switch Statements as Dispatch Tables
items.text: A switch with 20+ cases dispatching to different behaviour based on a type or status string is a code smell — it is a procedural dispatch table masquerading as OOP. The open-closed principle says new behaviour should be added by adding code (new classes), not modifying existing switch statements. Consider replacing large type-dispatch switches with polymorphism (subclasses/interfaces), strategy pattern, or Map-based dispatch.

items.title: Mixing Arrow and Colon Labels in the Same Switch
items.text: Java does not allow mixing arrow labels (case X ->) and colon labels (case X:) in the same switch block — it is a compile error. Choose one style per switch. Arrow style is preferred for switch expressions; colon style is the classic for switch statements. When migrating from classic to enhanced switch, convert the entire switch to arrow style at once.

sections.title: Java Switch Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews. Switch fall-through, switch expression, yield, and pattern matching are high-frequency topics.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between switch statement and switch expression in Java?
items.a: Switch statement: used for control flow. Executes a block of code for the matching case. Does not produce a value that can be assigned. Uses colon labels (case X:) and requires break to prevent fall-through. Has been in Java since version 1. Switch expression (Java 14+): produces a value — can be assigned, returned, or used in another expression. Uses arrow labels (case X ->) that prevent fall-through by default, or colon labels with yield to produce a value. Is exhaustive — every possible input must be covered (compile error otherwise). More concise and safer. Both can use: int, char, byte, short, String, enum as the selector. Switch expressions additionally support type patterns (Java 21+).

items.q: Q2. What is fall-through in switch? When is it useful?
items.a: Fall-through is when execution continues from a matched case into the next case without stopping because there is no break statement. Example: switch(x) { case 2: print('Two'); case 3: print('Three'); } — if x=2, both 'Two' and 'Three' are printed. Unintentional fall-through (forgotten break) is a very common bug. Intentional fall-through is used to group multiple cases that share the same result: case 6: case 7: System.out.println('Weekend'); break; — both 6 and 7 reach the same code. Enhanced switch (Java 14+) arrow labels eliminate fall-through entirely — each arrow case is independent. Best practice: always use break in classic switch cases unless fall-through is deliberate — and document it with a comment when it is.

items.q: Q3. What data types are supported as switch selector in Java?
items.a: Supported: byte, short, int, char (primitives). Their wrappers: Byte, Short, Integer, Character. String (Java 7+). enum (all versions). Any reference type for pattern matching (Java 21+). NOT supported: long, float, double, boolean, and their wrappers Long, Float, Double, Boolean. Why long is excluded: the JVM switch bytecodes (tableswitch and lookupswitch) are designed for 32-bit int values. Adding long would require significant bytecode changes for limited benefit — use if-else for long values. float/double are excluded because floating-point equality is unreliable — 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. boolean is excluded because if-else already serves that purpose cleanly.

items.q: Q4. What is the yield keyword in Java? How is it different from return?
items.a: yield (Java 14+) is used inside a switch expression to produce the value of the switch expression for that case. It is similar to return but scoped to the switch expression — it does not exit the enclosing method. return exits the entire method. Example: int result = switch(x) { case 1 -> { int val = compute(); yield val; } default -> 0; }; — yield val provides the value for the switch expression's case 1 arm, and then execution continues after the switch. yield is only valid in switch expressions — using it in a switch statement is a compile error. yield is not needed with single-expression arrow cases (case x -> value) — the value is implicit. yield is required in block arrow cases (case x -> { ... }) or colon cases (case x: ... yield value;).

items.q: Q5. Can we use String in a switch? Is the comparison case-sensitive?
items.a: Yes — String is supported in switch from Java 7. The comparison uses .equals() internally, so it IS case-sensitive. 'Monday' and 'monday' are different cases. Example: switch('start') { case 'START': ... } — does NOT match, default executes. To make it case-insensitive, normalize before switching: switch(input.toUpperCase()) { case 'START': ... }. Critical: passing null as the selector in String switch (classic or Java 14) throws NullPointerException at runtime — always null-check first, or use Java 21 case null in a pattern matching switch. Internally, Java translates String switch to a hashCode() check followed by equals() — this makes it efficient even with many cases.

items.q: Q6. What is pattern matching switch (Java 21)? How does it differ from classic switch?
items.a: Pattern matching switch (JEP 441, standard Java 21) extends switch to match on type patterns — similar to instanceof pattern matching but inside a switch. case Integer i -> matches if the selector is an Integer and binds it to i. case String s when s.length() > 5 -> guarded pattern — matches only if String AND length > 5. Classic switch: matches only constant values — literals, enum constants, or final variables. Limited to int/char/String/enum types. Pattern matching switch: matches types, subclasses, records, sealed types. Works on Object and any reference type. Supports guarded patterns (when clauses). Handles null directly (case null). Is exhaustive — compiler enforces all cases. No fall-through with arrow labels. Pattern matching switch replaces verbose if-instanceof chains and is the preferred modern dispatch mechanism in Java 21+.

Output: Two, Three, Default. Explanation: x = 2 matches case 2. Since there is no break after any case, execution falls through: case 2 prints 'Two', then execution continues to case 3 (prints 'Three'), then continues to default (prints 'Default'). This is classic fall-through — one of the most common Java beginner bugs. Fix: add break after each case: case 2: System.out.println('Two'); break; — then only 'Two' is printed. Alternatively, use enhanced switch: String r = switch(x) { case 2 -> 'Two'; ... } — no fall-through possible.

items.q: Q8. Can default be placed anywhere in a switch? Does position matter?
items.a: Yes — default can be placed anywhere in the switch block: at the beginning, middle, or end. Syntactically valid in all positions. However, position affects execution only when fall-through is involved. If a case matches, execution jumps to that case — default is skipped, regardless of its position. If no case matches, execution jumps to default. Example: switch(3) { default: print('D'); break; case 3: print('Three'); break; } — case 3 matches, 'Three' is printed, default is never reached. But: switch(3) { default: print('D'); case 3: print('Three'); } — case 3 matches, prints 'Three', and because default has no break it would fall through to... wait, default is before case 3 here, so after case 3 executes (no break), the switch ends. Convention: always place default last — it maximizes readability and avoids fall-through confusion.

items.q: Q9. What happens if the switch selector is null?
items.a: Classic switch (all versions) and enhanced switch expression without pattern matching: passing null throws NullPointerException at runtime — immediately, at the switch evaluation step. Example: String s = null; switch(s) { ... } — NullPointerException. Pattern matching switch (Java 21+): supports explicit case null. If case null is present, null is matched and handled. If case null is absent, null still throws NullPointerException — same behaviour as classic switch. Safe approach for pre-Java-21: if (s != null) before the switch. Safe approach for Java 21+: include case null -> 'handle null' inside a pattern matching switch. Null combined with default: case null, default -> 'catch-all' — handles both null and any unmatched value together.

items.q: Q10. Why can't we use long, float, or double as a switch selector?
items.a: long is not supported because the JVM switch bytecodes (tableswitch and lookupswitch) operate on int (32-bit) values. Adding long would require new bytecode instructions for limited practical benefit since long range values are rarely switched on. Use if-else for long comparisons. float and double are not supported because floating-point equality is imprecise — 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in IEEE 754 representation. A case 0.3: label might never match even for computations that 'should' equal 0.3. This would make float/double switch unreliable and error-prone. Use if/else with epsilon comparison for float/double. boolean is not supported because if/else already handles boolean branching idiomatically and adding boolean to switch would offer no benefit.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Java Switch Knowledge

blocks.text: Attempt each question independently before reading the answer — active recall is far more effective than passive reading.

items.a: Output: One or Two. x = 1 matches case 1. Case 1 has no statements and no break — it falls through to case 2. Case 2 prints 'One or Two' and breaks. This is intentional fall-through used to group cases 1 and 2 together. The same result can be achieved more cleanly with enhanced switch: case 1, 2 -> System.out.println('One or Two');

Output: Three. day = 3 matches case 3 — execution jumps directly to it (prints 'Three') and breaks. The default case is not executed even though it appears first — default only runs when NO case matches. If day were 5 (no matching case), execution would jump to default (prints 'Default'), then fall through to case 1 (prints 'One') because default has no break.

Does NOT compile. Error: switch expression does not cover all possible input values. A switch expression must be exhaustive — it must cover every possible value of the selector type. int has billions of possible values — only 1, 2, and 5 are covered. Fix: add a default case: default -> 'Other'; — this covers all remaining values. If the selector were an enum and all constants were covered, default would not be required. The exhaustiveness requirement is a safety feature of switch expressions — it prevents runtime cases where the switch cannot produce a value.

Output: Match! String switch uses .equals() for comparison which is case-sensitive. 'hello' exactly equals 'hello' — so case 'hello' matches and prints 'Match!'. Case 'Hello' (capital H) would only match if s were exactly 'Hello'. This demonstrates that String switch is case-sensitive. To perform case-insensitive matching, normalize before switching: switch (s.toLowerCase()) { case 'hello': ... }.

items.q: 6. Write a switch expression that returns the number of days in a month. Use String month names. Throw IllegalArgumentException for invalid input.

items.a:
Output:
Processing grade B
Result: B

x = 8 matches case 8. The case 8 arm has a block body ({}). Inside: grade = 'B' is assigned, 'Processing grade B' is printed, then yield grade produces 'B' as the value of the switch expression. yield provides the value for this block arm — without it, the block would have no value to yield and it would be a compile error. The switch expression's result is 'B', assigned to result. The second println prints 'Result: B'.

items.q: 8. Write a pattern matching switch (Java 21) that processes different event types: UserEvent(String userId), OrderEvent(String orderId, double amount), SystemEvent(String level). For OrderEvent with amount > 5000, print 'HIGH VALUE'. For SystemEvent with level CRITICAL, print 'ALERT'. Handle null.

sections.title: Conclusion — Switch: From Simple Dispatch to Powerful Pattern Matching

blocks.text: Java's switch has evolved from a simple multi-way branch with fall-through quirks into one of the most expressive features of modern Java. The classic switch statement is reliable for basic branching — but requires discipline with break. The enhanced switch expression (Java 14+) eliminates fall-through, produces values, and enforces exhaustiveness — making it the preferred form for most switching needs. The pattern matching switch (Java 21) brings type-safe dispatch, guarded conditions, and null handling into a single, concise construct.

Professional Java code favours switch expressions over classic switch statements for their safety and conciseness. It uses enum + switch expression for state machines, pattern matching switch for type-based dispatch over sealed hierarchies, and if-else when ranges or compound conditions are needed. Understanding when to use which form — and the pitfalls of fall-through and null — is a mark of Java mastery.

items.q: What is a switch statement in Java?
items.a: A switch statement is a multi-way branch control flow construct that evaluates one expression and executes the matching case block. It is a cleaner alternative to a long if-else-if chain when testing a single variable against multiple constant values. Syntax: switch (expression) { case value1: statements; break; ... default: statements; }. Supported types: int, char, byte, short, their wrappers, String (Java 7+), enum. Without break, execution falls through to the next case.

items.q: What is the difference between switch statement and switch expression in Java?
items.a: Switch statement: executes code, does not produce a value, uses colon labels (case X:), needs break to prevent fall-through. Switch expression (Java 14+): produces a value (assignable/returnable), uses arrow labels (case X ->) that prevent fall-through, or colon labels with yield. Switch expressions are exhaustive — compiler enforces that all cases are covered. Switch expressions are preferred — more concise, safer, and expression-oriented.

items.q: What is fall-through in Java switch?
items.a: Fall-through is when execution continues from a matched case into the next case without stopping because there is no break. Usually a bug (forgotten break). Intentional fall-through groups multiple cases sharing the same code: case 6: case 7: print('Weekend'); break. Enhanced switch (Java 14+) arrow labels eliminate fall-through entirely. Always use break in classic switch, or document intentional fall-through with a comment.

items.q: Can we use String in switch in Java?
items.a: Yes — String switch is supported since Java 7. Comparison uses .equals() — case-sensitive ('Monday' != 'monday'). Null causes NullPointerException — always null-check before switching on String, or use Java 21 case null in a pattern matching switch. Normalize with .toUpperCase() for case-insensitive matching. Internally uses hashCode() + equals() — efficient even with many cases.

items.q: What is the yield keyword in Java switch?
items.a: yield (Java 14+) produces a value from a switch expression's block case arm. It is like return but only for switch expressions — it does not exit the method. Required in: block arrow cases (case X -> { ... yield value; }) and colon cases (case X: yield value;). Not needed for single-expression arrow cases (case X -> value — yield is implicit). yield is only valid in switch expressions, not switch statements — using it in a switch statement is a compile error.
